I am 65 years old now, and my bones ache when the weather turns, but I know every inch of my 8 mu of flat land in Quzhou. My father taught me, and I have farmed this soil for over 40 years. We live on the North China Plain, so the only sensible thing is the double crop: winter wheat followed by summer maize. I already sowed the wheat last October after the autumn harvest, and it is greening up now. I will not gamble on new crops like vegetables or fruit—I am too old for that kind of risk, and my grandson needs tuition money. Wheat and maize give steady grain I can sell or store. I will use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed because the yield is better than the old traditional kinds, and everyone in the village buys them now. For fertilizer, I will put down compound fertilizer and urea the way the county extension man showed me years ago—enough nitrogen to make the crop strong, but not so much that it burns or wastes money. I will irrigate when the wheat is jointing, heading, and filling, and the maize twice when it is thirsty in July and August. I will spray pesticides two or three times when I see aphids or rust. For tillage, I hire the rotary tiller from the village cooperative because ploughing is too hard on my back and my old ox is long gone. I expect about 500–600 jin per mu for wheat and a bit more for maize if the rains come on time.
